meta.title: Who really said "When the anecdotes and the data disagree, the anecdotes are usually right"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, Jeff Bezos said it — on stage at the Bush Center's Forum on Leadership in April 2018, and again to Lex Fridman in 2023. Sourced and verified.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When the anecdotes and the data disagree, the anecdotes are usually right'?
meta.ogDescription: Jeff Bezos said it on stage at the Bush Center's Forum on Leadership, April 2018, and restated it on the Lex Fridman Podcast in 2023. Sourced.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: b. 1964 · Founder of Amazon and Blue Origin
answer.sourceLine: Bezos said it on stage in Dallas on 20 April 2018, closing the George W. Bush Presidential Center’s Forum on Leadership: “The thing I have noticed is when the anecdotes and the data disagree, the anecdotes are usually right.” He treats it as his own house rule — in December 2023 he introduced it to Lex Fridman as “a saying” of his and told the story behind it.

source.heading: Where it comes from

docMeta.dd: Closing Conversation, Forum on Leadership, George W. Bush Presidential Center

source.excerpt: The thing I have noticed is when the anecdotes and the data disagree, the anecdotes are usually right. There’s something wrong with the way you are measuring it.
trail: 20 April 2018 — Dallas. Bezos closed the Bush Center’s Forum on Leadership in conversation with Bush Center CEO Kenneth Hersh at SMU’s Moody Coliseum, an event SMU Magazine dates and places precisely ↗.

April 2018 — the line goes into print. Julie Bort quoted it for Business Insider: “The thing I have noticed is when the anecdotes and the data disagree, the anecdotes are usually right” — still readable in full ↗, and the citation Wikiquote uses for its sourced entry ↗.

December 2023 — he claims it as his own. On the Lex Fridman Podcast ↗ Bezos says “I have a saying, which is when the data and the anecdotes disagree, the anecdotes are usually right,” then tells the story of dialling Amazon’s customer-service line mid-meeting to test a wait-time metric.
source.excerptNote: The popular short form simply drops Bezos’s lead-in. His 2023 restatement flips the order of the two nouns — “when the data and the anecdotes disagree” — but the payoff clause is identical.

author.name: Jeff Bezos
author.heading: Jeff Bezos
author.metaLine: b. 12 January 1964 · Founder of Amazon and Blue Origin; owner of The Washington Post
author.bio: Jeffrey Preston Bezos was born in Albuquerque, New Mexico, and founded Amazon in 1994, serving as its chief executive until July 2021, when he moved to executive chairman. He also founded the spaceflight company Blue Origin and bought The Washington Post in 2013. His management vocabulary — two-pizza teams, one-way doors, the six-page memo, disagree and commit — has been quoted, borrowed and garbled across the business world, which is exactly why a line like this one needs a paper trail.

Quoted in Julie Bort, “Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos explains his famous one-character emails, known to strike fear in manager’s hearts,” Business Insider, April 2018. Restated by Bezos in “Jeff Bezos: Amazon and Blue Origin,” Lex Fridman Podcast #405, December 2023 (official transcript).

misattribution.heading: What gets tangled up with it
misattribution.intro: This one is not a fake — the words are Bezos’s and the occasion is documented. What goes wrong is bookkeeping: the line gets filed under the wrong name, blended with older adages that sound like it, and reproduced in two different word orders.

items.why: Anderson’s book quotes Bezos, and quotation databases index the container rather than the speaker — Goodreads lists the line under Anderson’s name ↗, with “Bezos quote:” buried inside the quotation text itself.

Quote Investigator names Wolfinger the leading candidate for “The plural of anecdote is data,” which he said he uttered during the 1969–70 academic year in a Stanford graduate seminar — and that page does not mention Bezos at all ↗. Same subject matter, unrelated origin.

items.who: Kenneth Kernaghan and P. K. Kuruvilla
items.why: The inverted proverb — “the plural of anecdote is not data” — has its own trail: QI’s earliest strong match is a 1982 article in Canadian Public Administration ↗, an attribution QI still calls provisional.

“When the anecdotes and the data disagree” is the 2018 Dallas wording; “when the data and the anecdotes disagree” is how he put it to Lex Fridman in 2023. Neither is a corruption of the other — the 2023 transcript shows the swap in his own mouth ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The saying is Bezos’s. The oldest public airing we could confirm is the Bush Center stage on 20 April 2018, the citation Wikiquote carries in its sourced quotes ↗.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: It reads like an anti-data slogan, and it is the opposite of one. Bezos’s point is that a conflict between what customers say and what the dashboard says is almost never a story about lying customers — it is a bug report about the dashboard. As he put it in 2023: “it’s usually not that the data is being miscollected, it’s usually that you’re not measuring the right thing.”

The story he attaches to it is the reason the line travels. Amazon’s metrics claimed customers reached phone support in under 60 seconds; the complaints said otherwise. In a weekly business review, with the executive responsible defending the number, Bezos picked up the phone, dialled the 1-800 line, and the room sat in silence. The wait ran past ten minutes. The metric was measuring something — just not the thing anyone cared about.
context.detailsSummary: How the customer-service call actually went
detailsBody: Bezos dates the episode only to “very early in the history of Amazon” and gives no year; the retelling comes from the December 2023 Lex Fridman interview, not from a contemporaneous record.

In his account the demonstration “set off a whole chain of events where we started measuring it right,” and he files it under truth-telling rather than analytics: “you have to seek truth even when it’s uncomfortable.”
context.pull: The anecdotes were not beating the data. They caught the data measuring the wrong thing.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Jeff Bezos page carries, among its sourced quotes, "The thing I have noticed is when the anecdotes and the data disagree, the anecdotes are usually right. There's something wrong with the way you are measuring it," cited to Julie Bort, Business Insider (21 April 2018).

Julie Bort's Business Insider article (April 2018) quotes Bezos verbatim as saying "The thing I have noticed is when the anecdotes and the data disagree, the anecdotes are usually right," and identifies the setting as an on-stage interview at the George W. Bush Presidential Center.

The official transcript of Lex Fridman Podcast #405 records Bezos saying "I have a saying, which is when the data and the anecdotes disagree, the anecdotes are usually right," adding "it's usually not that the data is being miscollected, it's usually that you're not measuring the right thing," and telling the story of calling Amazon's 1-800 customer-service line during a weekly business review, where the wait ran "more than 10 minutes" against a metric of under 60 seconds.
SMU Magazine confirms Jeff Bezos spoke on 20 April 2018 at Moody Coliseum, SMU, in the Bush Center's Forum on Leadership, moderated by Bush Center CEO Kenneth Hersh.

Quote Investigator names Raymond Wolfinger the leading candidate for coining "The plural of anecdote is data," which Wolfinger said he uttered during the 1969-70 academic year in a Stanford graduate seminar; the page does not mention Jeff Bezos.

Quote Investigator's earliest strong match for "the plural of anecdote is not data" is a 1982 article by Kenneth Kernaghan and P. K. Kuruvilla in Canadian Public Administration, an attribution QI describes as provisional.

Goodreads files the quote "...when the anecdotes and the data disagree, the anecdotes are usually right. There's something wrong with the way you're measuring it" under author Steve Anderson and the book The Bezos Letters, rather than under Jeff Bezos.

Jeff Bezos was born 12 January 1964 in Albuquerque, New Mexico; he founded Amazon in 1994, stepped down as CEO in July 2021 to become executive chairman, founded Blue Origin, and bought The Washington Post in 2013.
YouTube hosts a video titled "Forum on Leadership: A Conversation with Jeff Bezos."
